strengths: Clear motivation and well-scoped problem formulation addressing the shortcomings of pure prompt-based text-to-image editing (fragility, inability to model continuous causal attributes, and lack of causal graph awareness) for counterfactual generation.

Methodologically sound design combining lightweight adapter injection with Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI) and Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss, which effectively enforces attribute disentanglement in the cross-attention space.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse domains (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA face attributes, and ADNI brain MRI), showing substantial improvements in perceptual realism (FID), null-intervention composition (LPIPS/MAE), and counterfactual effectiveness.
Thorough ablation studies and analysis, dissecting the roles of PAI, CTC, attention guidance, classifier-free guidance scales, and inversion steps both quantitatively and qualitatively.
weaknesses: Reliance on a strictly known and correct causal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) over fully observed semantic attributes; the manuscript does not analyze sensitivity or robustness against graph misspecification or unobserved confounding.

On the CelebA and ADNI benchmarks (Tables 2–4), the comparisons are limited primarily to VAE, HVAE, and GAN baselines from the Melistas et al. benchmark suite, omitting recent diffusion-based counterfactual methods (such as DiffSCM, CausalDiffAE, or semantic-abduction diffusion) that were only benchmarked on the synthetic Pendulum dataset.

Generating at 256x256 and subsequently bicubic downsampling to low resolutions (e.g., 64x64 for CelebA, 94x94 for Pendulum) to match prior benchmarks may introduce evaluation discrepancies or inflate relative FID improvements against models trained directly at native lower resolutions.

Instantiating a half-scale replica of the U-Net denoiser adds non-trivial parameter and memory overhead compared to parameter-efficient fine-tuning alternatives (e.g., low-rank adaptation or lightweight cross-attention adapters).

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated framework: Adapting frozen, large-scale text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models with a lightweight causal adapter avoids expensive scratch pre-training while leveraging the strong priors of foundation diffusion models for counterfactual generation.

Effective attribute regularization: The combination of Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI) and Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss elegantly addresses the issue of attribute entanglement and spurious correlations in diffusion cross-attention spaces.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated on three distinct datasets spanning synthetic mechanics (Pendulum), human faces (CelebA), and clinical neuroimaging (ADNI), exhibiting clear quantitative gains in realism (FID), null-intervention reconstruction (LPIPS/MAE), and counterfactual manipulation accuracy.

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analyses: The paper provides insightful analyses including cross-attention map visualizations, guidance scale sweeps, DDIM step sensitivity, and an honest discussion of evaluation limitations (e.g., OOD failure modes of pre-trained evaluation classifiers on rare counterfactual combinations like bearded females).
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons on complex benchmarks: On CelebA and ADNI (Tables 2, 3, 4), the comparison baselines are predominantly older architectures (VAE, HVAE, and GAN from Melistas et al., 2024). While CausalDiffAE and DisDiffAE are evaluated on the synthetic Pendulum benchmark, recent diffusion-based counterfactual baselines (such as DiffSCM, CausalDiffAE, or DiffAE variants) are not systematically benchmarked on CelebA or ADNI, making it difficult to fully disentangle the advantage of the causal adapter architecture from the advantage of using a billion-parameter pretrained Stable Diffusion backbone.

Potential domain gap in medical imaging: Stable Diffusion v1.5 is pretrained on natural images. While the adapter enables synthesis on ADNI brain MRI scans, generating at 256x256 RGB and downsampling to 192x192 grayscale introduces questions regarding clinical fidelity that go beyond standard natural image FID metrics.

Notational consistency between vanilla and regularized variants: In Section 2.3 (Eq. 4 and Algorithm 1), causal attributes are injected by concatenation/addition with latent representations ($z_t \oplus Y$), whereas in Section 2.4 (Eq. 7) and Algorithm 3, attributes are routed via the cross-attention token embeddings $V(Y)$. Explicitly detailing whether the direct latent injection $z_t \oplus Y$ is completely replaced by or combined with PAI in the final model would enhance clarity.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing key limitations of text-to-image (T2I) editing methods (e.g., Null-Text Inversion, MCPL) in handling continuous numerical variables, causal dependencies, and attribute entanglement.
The proposed modular adapter formulation leverages frozen Stable Diffusion priors while avoiding expensive end-to-end retraining or full diffusion model fine-tuning.

The introduction of Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI) and Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss provides an intuitive mechanism to ground scalar causal attributes into cross-attention spaces and enforce factor disentanglement.
Extensive qualitative visualizations and ablations across three domains (synthetic Pendulum, human faces CelebA, and brain MRI ADNI), including attention maps, guidance scales, and denoising steps.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons on CelebA and ADNI: Tables 2, 3, and 4 compare the proposed method (which builds on a massively pretrained Stable Diffusion v1.5 backbone) only against older generative baselines (VAE, HVAE, GAN). Key diffusion-based counterfactual baselines cited in the text (such as DiffSCM, CausalDiffAE, or semantic-abduction diffusion models) are missing from the real-world evaluations.

Evaluation disparity from pretraining and resolution: CelebA images are evaluated at 64x64 and ADNI at 192x192, but Causal-Adapter generates at 256x256 using SD v1.5 and downsamples. Baseline models trained from scratch at native lower resolutions are at an intrinsic disadvantage regarding FID and LPIPS compared to a large-scale web-pretrained foundation model.

Decoupled SCM and limited technical novelty in causal abduction: The causal modeling consists of fitting an independent SCM (additive noise model or normalizing flow) purely on low-dimensional tabular attributes Y, after which updated attributes are fed as conditional tokens into the adapter. The image-level abduction relies purely on standard DDIM deterministic inversion without causal identifiability guarantees on the image latents themselves.

Notational and formulation inconsistencies: In Section 2.3, Eq. (4) presents spatial/latent addition $z_t \oplus Y$ for the adapter input, whereas Section 2.4 and Algorithms 3–4 transition to feeding $Y$ exclusively via text embeddings $V(Y)$. Clarifying the exact architectural progression between the vanilla and regularized variants would improve soundness.
Reliance on fully known causal graphs without sensitivity analysis to graph misspecification or unobserved confounders.

strengths: Compelling and practical formulation: Adapting frozen text-to-image (T2I) diffusion backbones for counterfactual generation avoids the heavy computational burden of retraining diffusion models from scratch while capitalizing on the high perceptual quality of modern foundational models.

Well-motivated regularizations: The proposed Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI) and Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss effectively bridge the gap between continuous/discrete attribute conditioning and spatial diffusion latents, mitigating attribute leakage and spurious correlations as verified by cross-attention visualizations.

Comprehensive and convincing empirical evaluation: The method is validated across four distinct domains (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, and ADNI brain MRI), demonstrating consistent improvements across standard counterfactual benchmarks in effectiveness, realism (FID), composition (LPIPS), and minimality (CLD).

Strong architectural generalization and extensibility: The authors show successful adaptation not only on U-Net based Stable Diffusion (v1.5) with DDIM inversion, but also on Diffusion Transformers (SD3) using FlowEdit, as well as an interesting preliminary extension to differentiable causal graph discovery.
weaknesses: Decoupling of the attribute SCM from visual abduction: The structural causal model is estimated purely over the low-dimensional observed attribute space $Y$ via additive noise models (Eq. 1–2). The image-level abduction relies purely on deterministic DDIM inversion/FlowEdit, meaning theoretical counterfactual identifiability at the visual level remains heuristic rather than formally guaranteed.

Rigidity of prompt templating: The PAI mechanism requires rigid, slot-based prompt structures (e.g., 'a human is @ and * and &'), which somewhat limits open-form natural language conditioning and requires knowing the full set of attributes a priori.

Presentation of variance in main results: In Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4 in the main body, metric variances across multiple seeds are omitted (though partially included in the appendix in Table 12); reporting confidence intervals in the main tables would strengthen reproducibility and statistical significance.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Adapting large, frozen text-to-image (T2I) diffusion backbones for causal counterfactual generation without requiring computationally expensive full fine-tuning or training from scratch is an important and practical research direction.

Well-motivated modular design: Decoupling the explicit structural causal model (SCM) estimation over semantic attributes from image synthesis, and introducing Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI) alongside Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss effectively addresses attribute entanglement and cross-factor leakage.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The approach is evaluated across diverse benchmarks spanning synthetic physics (Pendulum), real-world faces (CelebA, CelebA-HQ), and safety-critical medical data (ADNI MRI scans), consistently demonstrating solid improvements in intervention effectiveness, image realism (FID), and identity preservation.

Extensive ablations and analyses: The manuscript provides thorough analyses of guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention maps, backbone generalization (extending to SD3 / DiT with FlowEdit), and exploratory causal graph discovery.
weaknesses: Reliance on fully observed attribute annotations: The SCM operates directly on pre-defined, fully observed attribute labels, meaning the framework cannot easily handle unobserved confounders or settings where dense attribute annotations are unavailable.

Approximate counterfactual identifiability: As discussed in Appendix F, counterfactual generation relies on DDIM inversion (or FlowEdit), which serves as an empirical approximation to the abduction of exogenous noise without theoretical identifiability guarantees.

Ablation against standard controllable diffusion baselines: While the paper compares extensively against causal generative models (HVAE, DiffCounter, CausalDiffAE), it lacks a direct baseline comparing against a standard ControlNet/T2I-Adapter pipeline coupled with simple SCM propagation at inference time to fully isolate the unique impact of PAI and CTC versus architecture.

Notational ambiguity in early sections: Eq. (3) writes $z_t \oplus Y$ into the adapter before introducing Prompt-Aligned Injection in Section 2.4, which can briefly confuse readers regarding how low-dimensional vector attributes are spatially fused with the latent feature map.

strengths: Practical and modular framework: Adapting frozen pre-trained text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) via a lightweight adapter avoids costly end-to-end retraining while preserving generative fidelity.

Effective disentanglement regularizations: The proposed Prompt-Aligned Injection (PAI) allows continuous numeric attribute manipulation via token projection, and the Conditioned Token Contrastive (CTC) loss effectively mitigates attribute entanglement and spurious cross-factor leakage.

Broad empirical coverage: The paper provides extensive experiments across synthetic benchmarks (Pendulum), real-world faces (CelebA, CelebA-HQ), and clinical MRI data (ADNI), supported by detailed qualitative visualizations and attention map analyses.

Architectural flexibility: The authors show that the proposed framework generalizes across different generative paradigms and backbones, including both U-Net (SD 1.5 with DDIM) and Diffusion Transformer (SD3 with FlowEdit).
Detailed ablation and parameter sensitivity analysis: The paper includes thorough investigations on the individual effects of PAI, CTC, classifier-free guidance scales, and DDIM steps.
weaknesses: Decoupled SCM and heuristic abduction: The structural causal model (Eqs. 1–2) is fitted exclusively on the low-dimensional tabular/scalar attribute vector Y and is entirely decoupled from the image domain. Abduction is approximated via standard DDIM inversion rather than structural abduction over true latent exogenous variables of the image, meaning the theoretical SCM integration into image generation is limited.

Unfair baseline capacity comparison: In Tables 2 (CelebA) and 3 (ADNI), Causal-Adapter is evaluated primarily against small VAE, HVAE, and GAN baselines trained from scratch. The significant gains in FID and LPIPS are largely attributable to the massive pre-trained knowledge base of Stable Diffusion rather than the causal adapter module alone. Modern diffusion counterfactual baselines (e.g., DiffCounter, CausalDiffAE, DiffSCM) should have been benchmarked on CelebA and ADNI as well.

Formulation ambiguity between spatial injection and prompt conditioning: Eq. (3) suggests causal attributes are injected directly into the latent space via concatenation/addition ($z_t \oplus Y$), whereas Section 2.4 (Eqs. 5–6) and Algorithm 1 (line 13) describe conditioning the adapter via cross-attention on $V(Y)$. Clarification is needed on how the spatial dimensions of $z_t$ interact with scalar attributes $Y$ in the adapter architecture.

Overstated causal structure learning contribution: In Appendix G, the claim that Causal-Adapter unifies causal discovery and counterfactual generation is overstated; the discovery phase is simply standard differentiable DAG discovery (NOTEARS/DAGMA) applied strictly to the tabular attribute metadata $Y$, completely independent of the visual adapter and diffusion backbone.
